concepts.title: Sources of Data: Primary and Secondary
concepts.definition: Data for a statistical study may be collected first-hand from the field -- primary data -- or drawn from published and recorded sources -- secondary data. Primary collection gives fit and freshness at a cost; secondary use is cheap and quick but limited by someone else's purpose and definitions.
concepts.key_idea: Ask it yourself or borrow it from records -- primary costs time, secondary costs control.
concepts.textbook_ref: kest102.txt sources sections (primary data, secondary data, merits and demerits, published sources of secondary data)
question_patterns: distinguish primary data from secondary data with examples
in class 11 collection of data: when should secondary data be preferred
name the sources from which secondary data are obtained
what are the merits and demerits of collecting primary data
is census data primary or secondary for a researcher explain
choose the data source for a given study and justify

solution_steps.explain: If the investigator generates the data for the study at hand, it is primary; if already collected by others, it is secondary.
Primary data fit the purpose exactly but need money, time and trained staff; secondary data is economical but possibly outdated or misfit.
Secondary data must be tested for reliability, adequacy and suitability before acceptance.

concepts.title: Modes of Collecting Primary Data
concepts.definition: Primary data arrive by three main modes: personal interviews where the investigator questions respondents face to face; mailed questionnaires that respondents fill themselves; and telephone or telephoned interviews for quick reach. Choice depends on area, literacy, cost and accuracy needed.
concepts.key_idea: Meet, mail or phone -- each mode trades cost against accuracy and coverage.
concepts.textbook_ref: kest102.txt modes sections (personal interview, mailed questionnaire, telephone interview, merits demerits of each mode)
question_patterns: compare personal interviews with mailed questionnaires
in class 11 collection of data: when is a telephone interview suitable
what qualities should a good questionnaire have
why do personal interviews give better response rates
state the limitations of the mailed questionnaire method
choose a mode of data collection for a given survey and justify

solution_steps.explain: Literate, far-flung respondents suit mailed questionnaires; illiterate or hesitant ones need personal interviews.
Personal presence lifts response and quality but costs travel and time; the telephone is quick but shallow.
Whatever the mode, questions must be short, clear, non-leading and sequenced from easy to harder.

concepts.title: Pilot Survey, Census and Sampling Frames
concepts.definition: Before the main collection, a pilot survey trials the questionnaire on a small group to expose confusing questions. The study then chooses between a census -- covering every unit of the population -- and a sample survey -- studying a selected few to represent the whole; the sampling frame lists the units from which the sample is drawn.
concepts.key_idea: Try it small, then cover all -- or let a well-chosen few speak for the whole.
concepts.textbook_ref: kest102.txt pilot census sections (pilot survey, census, sample survey, population, sampling frame, merits of sampling)
question_patterns: what is a pilot survey and why is it conducted
in class 11 collection of data: distinguish census from sample survey
when must a census be used instead of sampling
state the merits of a sample survey over a census
plan a pilot study for a given questionnaire

solution_steps.explain: A small trial reveals ambiguous wording and logistical snags, letting the questionnaire be repaired cheaply.
A census reaches every unit -- exhaustive but costly; a sample saves resources but demands representativeness.
Prepare the list of population units from which the sample will be selected, ensuring it is complete and current.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A researcher must survey 2000 farmers spread across villages with mixed literacy. Which mode of collection suits best and why?

solution_template.explain: Mixed literacy rules out mailed questionnaires that demand reading and writing.
Personal interviews, with the investigator reading out questions, reach everyone accurately.
Travel and time are the price of quality here -- the trade-off favours accuracy.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A college wants to know the average pocket money of its 4000 students in one week. Census or sample? Justify and describe the procedure.

solution_template.explain: A census of 4000 is possible but heavy; a well-drawn sample of, say, 400 gives a good estimate cheaply.
The roll of all 4000 students is the sampling frame from which names are selected.
Trialling the questionnaire on 20 students catches unclear items before the main survey.
